Turning 90 degrees at a corner requires the robot to decelerate, rotate, and accelerate again. A smooth curve lets the robot carry speed through the turn.

BezierCurve takes three poses: start, control, end. The curve bends toward the control point but doesn't pass through it.

A Bezier curve uses a parameter t that goes from 0 to 1 as the robot moves:

At t=0: robot is at the start point.

At t=0.5: robot is pulled halfway toward the control point.

At t=1: robot arrives at the end point.

The control point acts like a magnet — the closer t gets to 0.5, the stronger the pull. That's what creates the curve shape.

Typing control point coordinates by hand is hard. Use the Pedro Pathing Visualizer instead:

Click to place start and end points. Drag the control point to shape the curve. See it update in real time. Export the Java code and paste it into your OpMode.

Teams don't guess control point positions — they design visually.

Open BezierCurveOpMode.java.

The skeleton has a private Follower field.

Create the Follower with Constants.createFollower(hardwareMap). Set its pose with follower.setPose(new Pose(70.75, 70.75, 0)).

Position the robot: left-click drag near center, right-click to face 0° (right).

Build a PathChain with a single BezierCurve:

new BezierCurve(
    new Pose(70.75, 70.75, 0),
    new Pose(70.75, 120.75, 0),
    new Pose(70.75, 170.75, 0)
)

Use setTangentHeadingInterpolation() so the robot faces the direction of the curve.

Always add .setGlobalDeceleration() before .build().

Schedule: new FollowPathCommand(follower, chain).

Override run() to call super.run() and then follower.update() every tick so the Follower drives the curve.

Start the OpMode. The robot follows a smooth arc.

Try changing the control point in the Visualizer — farther from the line for a deeper bend, closer for a shallower one.
